title: ASML and the West's technology dilemma
gist: ASML is the world's sole supplier of EUV lithography, making the Dutch firm the single chokepoint in the AI chip race — but reports that China has begun producing its own DUV machines, heavily based on Dutch technology, dented ASML's share price and exposed the core dilemma: export controls reliably work in the short run while spurring measurable, persistent Chinese R&D and patenting in the medium run.

insights.claim: ASML of Veldhoven is the world's sole supplier of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithographic systems, so every leading chipmaker — TSMC, Samsung and Intel — depends on one Dutch firm to produce the most advanced chips.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: A single-supplier chokepoint means ASML order flow and export-licence news is a leading indicator for the entire advanced-chip and AI hardware complex.
insights.quote: ASML has a decent claim to be the most significant European company that the fewest people have heard of.

insights.claim: The chokepoint is asymmetric by node: alternative sources exist for deep ultraviolet (DUV) machines capable of producing less advanced chips, while EUV has no second source at all.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Controls bite hardest at the leading edge; trailing-edge capacity is far more contestable, so China's substitution path runs DUV-first.
insights.locator: While there are other sources of deep ultraviolet

insights.claim: Anyone producing the chips required to power the AI race is reliant on ASML, making a Dutch company the effective gatekeeper of global AI compute.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Political risk in the Netherlands, not just Taiwan, belongs in any AI supply-chain risk model.
insights.quote: Anyone producing the chips required to power the AI race finds themselves reliant on the Dutch firm.

themes.theme: Export controls and the China response

insights.claim: Three successive US administrations — Trump's first term, Biden, and Trump again — have pressured the Dutch government into progressively tightening ASML's China sales, squeezing off not only EUV but also the more advanced DUV models.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: The ratchet is bipartisan and multi-administration, so investors should price continuation rather than reversal of ASML China restrictions.
insights.locator: Beginning during President Trump's first term

insights.claim: Reports last month that China has begun producing its own DUV machines, heavily based on Dutch technology, were enough to seriously dent ASML's share price and alarm US geopolitical strategists.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Chinese domestic lithography milestones are now a direct, tradable risk factor for ASML equity, not just a policy headline.
insights.locator: Reports last month that China has begun

insights.claim: China's lithographic industry is roughly a decade behind ASML but catching up rapidly, which is striking given the Dutch firm enjoyed a four-decade head start.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: The rate of catch-up, not the current gap, is what should compress ASML's terminal-value assumptions for the China market.
insights.quote: China’s lithographic industry is perhaps a decade behind ASML, but, given the Dutch firm had a four-decade head start, it is catching up rapidly.

insights.claim: Empirical work on US export restrictions on China across the 2000s and 2010s shows the tools work well in the short run — Chinese imports of restricted items fall materially — but in the medium term restricted Chinese firms respond by raising R&D spend and patent counts.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Controls buy time, not permanence; position for a multi-year window of Western advantage followed by domestic Chinese substitutes in restricted categories.
insights.locator: Recent work looking at US restrictions

insights.claim: Denying ASML the ability to export to China has almost certainly undercut Chinese efforts in the AI race, but at the price of potentially creating a stronger rather than weaker Chinese AI and chipmaking sector.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: The bull case for Chinese semicap equipment names is literally the mechanism of Western sanctions; treat controls as a subsidy to domestic Chinese toolmakers.
insights.locator: In other words, policymakers have a careful balance

insights.claim: Technology-transfer anxiety is as old as modern economic growth: during the Industrial Revolution Britain passed parliamentary statutes banning both the export of key machinery and the emigration of skilled artisans.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Today's chip controls are a re-run of a well-documented policy genre whose outcomes are already known from history.

insights.claim: Samuel Slater evaded British emigration restrictions by declaring himself a farmer, and by 1793 was running a New England mill that copied British water-frame technology plus British organisational and management techniques — hailed by Andrew Jackson as father of the American factory system and denounced at home as 'Slater the traitor'.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Human capital leakage, not just hardware, is the transfer channel — a reminder that engineer poaching defeats machine-level export controls.
insights.quote: Back in Britain he was known as ‘Slater the traitor’.
insights.locator: Take, as one prominent example, the case of Samuel Slater

insights.claim: The British blockade leaked fast in practice: the water frame first used in England in 1769 was in France by 1779 and the Netherlands by 1785, and at least 1,000 British artisans are known to have moved to France between 1710 and 1800.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: A decade of diffusion lag is the realistic ceiling for controls — useful for timing horizons on 'sovereign' tech investment theses.
insights.quote: The technology blockade was always porous, never absolute.
insights.locator: The technology blockade was always porous

insights.claim: Britain abandoned the controls once its own interests flipped: the emigration ban was dropped in the mid-1820s and machinery export controls were repealed altogether in the 1840s as manufacturers became keen to sell technology overseas amid the swing to free trade.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Export-control regimes end when domestic exporters' commercial interest outweighs the strategic rationale — watch for ASML and Western semicap lobbying as the leading edge of that flip.
insights.locator: Eventually, the British government changed track

insights.claim: The consensus of economic historians is that even leaky controls raised the cost of replicating Britain's approach — governments cannot stop technology being used abroad but can materially delay its introduction.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Delay, measured in years to decades, is the correct success metric for chip controls — not permanent denial.
insights.quote: The British government could not stop technology from being used in France, the Netherlands or the United States but they could materially delay its introduction.
insights.locator: The consensus view of economic historians

themes.theme: Cold War controls as the closer analogue

insights.claim: Cold War technology blocks were more successful than the Industrial Revolution version: from the late 1940s Western economies controlled not only military technology but industrial goods and processes, especially in computing and semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: The computing/semiconductor sector has the strongest historical record of controllability — supporting the case that chip controls are unusually effective relative to other embargoes.
insights.locator: Cold War efforts to block technology transfer

insights.claim: Workarounds during the Cold War ran through third- or even fourth-party transaction chains and old-fashioned industrial espionage, yet researchers find good evidence the controls were one of the factors holding back Soviet and Eastern Bloc productivity through the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s.
insights.speaker: Duncan Weldon
insights.so_what: Transshipment through third countries is the predictable evasion route — enforcement headlines on intermediaries are the tell for how binding controls really are.
